groups.title: Template and Layout Architecture
groups.question: Your recipe pages repeat the same card markup and formatting logic everywhere, and users get no feedback after saving. Explain how views, partials and helpers keep this clean.

followUps.ERB syntax and view rendering lifecycle: What is the difference between <%= %> and <% %> in ERB?
followUps.Partials and view helpers for reuse: When would you use a partial and when a helper?
followUps.Flash messages and user feedback pattern: Where should flash messages be rendered and why?

evidence.text: <%= %> runs Ruby and outputs the result into the HTML.
<% %> runs Ruby without outputting, for loops and conditions.
The action's template is rendered first and then inserted into the layout.
Partials are reusable chunks of markup, named with a leading underscore.
Helpers are Ruby methods for view logic like formatting.
Moving logic out of templates into helpers makes it easier to test.

notEnough: Only saying both are for reuse.

evidence.text: Flash messages last for one request after a redirect.
Rendering them in the layout makes them show on any page.
Notices and alerts distinguish success from errors.

groups.title: Forms and Parameters
groups.question: A user edits their profile and manages to make themselves an admin through the form, and a recipe form must also create its ingredients. Explain how Rails forms and parameters should work.

followUps.Nested forms and complex data submission: How do nested attributes let one form save a recipe and its ingredients?

evidence.text: form_with builds forms tied to a model, including the security token.
Strong parameters require you to list which fields may be assigned.
This stops users from setting fields like admin by adding them to the request.

notEnough: Only saying strong parameters are required.

evidence.text: accepts_nested_attributes_for lets a model save associated records.
fields_for renders the fields for the associated records.
The nested fields must also be permitted in strong parameters.

notEnough: Only saying you use nested forms.

groups.title: Asset Management
groups.question: Your CSS and JavaScript are not cached properly by browsers and you want to use Tailwind. Explain how Rails handles assets and CSS builds.

followUps.Rails asset pipeline with Sprockets: What does the asset pipeline do to your files?
followUps.Importing CSS with cssbundling-rails: How does cssbundling-rails add Tailwind or Sass?

evidence.text: It combines and minifies CSS and JavaScript.
It adds a fingerprint to file names based on their contents.
Fingerprints let browsers cache files for a long time and fetch new ones after changes.
It runs a Node-based build step for the CSS tool.
It supports Tailwind, Sass and PostCSS.
The built CSS is written to app/assets/builds for the asset pipeline to serve.

groups.title: Frontend Integration
groups.question: You want to add a little JavaScript to your Rails app, and later you need a few npm packages. Explain the two approaches.

followUps.importmap-rails for JavaScript modules: How do import maps load JavaScript without a bundler?
followUps.jsbundling-rails with esbuild or webpack: When would you switch to jsbundling with esbuild?

evidence.text: Import maps use the browser's built-in module loading.
Packages are pinned to URLs, locally or from a CDN.
There is no bundling step, which keeps setup simple.
jsbundling adds a JavaScript bundling step.
It suits apps that need many npm packages or a build step.
esbuild is very fast, while webpack offers more configuration.
